tagline.text: World-famous dawn dives with thresher sharks

location.label: Location
location.text: Offshore from Malapascua Island in northern Cebu, at Kimud Shoal and Monad Shoal

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: December–July dry season (threshers appear year-round; April–May is peak-season crowded)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 2–3 dives starting at dawn, about 5–7 hours

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,000~7,000 (2–3 dives including various fees, per person)

children.text: Malapascua Island in northern Cebu is one of the few places where you can see large thresher sharks on dawn dives almost every day. An Advanced Open Water certification is recommended, and the sharks have recently shifted to Kimud Shoal, so dives now center there.

Malapascua is a small island about 30–45 minutes by bangka from the northern tip of mainland Cebu. There are no cars, so people walk the sandy paths or ride motorbikes, and dive shops line the beach. The island is famous among divers for the pelagic thresher shark. Normally an open-ocean shark, here it rises at first light to "cleaning stations" on deep reefs, where cleaner wrasse pick parasites off its body, and you can watch this up close.

A pelagic thresher is usually about 3 m long and hunts by stunning small fish with its tail, which is as long as its body. According to Wikipedia, the species is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List. At the cleaning station the sharks swim slowly in circles near the bottom while cleaner fish pick at the tail and pelvic-fin areas. They are known not to be aggressive toward people, but they are wild sharks, so you must follow the dive shop's rules.

Dives leave before the darkness lifts. Many reviews say you meet at the shop around 4:30 AM and the boat leaves around 5 AM. The boat goes to one of two places. One is Kimud Shoal, where the threshers are known to have moved around 2022 and now appear almost daily. The other is Monad Shoal, the former thresher hotspot, where threshers are now seen only rarely and many guides say tiger sharks occasionally appear instead.

Because threshers appear all year, there is no fixed off-season. However, trips can be canceled because of weather, and Advanced Open Water (AOW) or higher is generally recommended. Fees and rules differ by shop, so confirm the exact current terms before booking. If you are not certified, look first into an intro scuba course and shallow snorkeling rather than this trip. Malapascua also offers other diving beyond threshers: the tunnel at Gato Island, shallow coral gardens and macro diving for small creatures, and many divers stay several more days after the sharks. Plan at least 3 nights and 4 days, and treat the first day as a travel day.
Thresher sharks often gather at the cleaning stations in the early morning, which is why dives leave before sunrise. You can reportedly see the sharks circling slowly in sunlit water.

Known today as the place where threshers are seen most often. One guide says the top of the reef is about 12–14 m and the cleaning stations lie at about 20–28 m. Reviewers say the boat ride takes about an hour.

Once the thresher hotspot, it has become a place where they are now rare. One guide says tiger sharks occasionally appear instead, and you also see other sharks such as whitetip reef sharks and rays. Reviewers say the boat ride is about 20–25 minutes.

Near Malapascua, Gato Island has a tunnel about 10 m deep and 10–15 m long, where whitetip reef sharks are known to be seen. Because it is an overhead environment, advanced certification is often recommended.

No flash or strobes, stay neutrally buoyant, and do not touch the reef. Stay behind the rope line and do not chase or touch the sharks. These rules are part of the effort to keep the sharks coming back to this spot. One review adds that noise makers, reef hooks and pointer sticks are not used either.

Many guides say threshers appear all year. One guide gives water temperatures of about 26–27°C in January and February and 28–30°C from March to December. Visibility is given as about 15–30 m or more.
Dives often end around midday, leaving the afternoon to relax on the beach or try other activities. One review says the dive day ends at 1–2 PM.
Gather at the dive shop, check your equipment and register. At the briefing, be sure to listen to the rules for dealing with sharks.
The boat departs. Reviewers say Kimud Shoal takes about an hour to reach, and a light breakfast may be served on board.
First dive. Wait for the threshers to appear at about 20–28 m near the cleaning stations.
Surface interval. One review mentions a shark breaching the surface at times.
Second dive. Observe the sharks again at the same reef at a different time.
Some operators offer a third dive at Monad Shoal or another site. It varies by shop.
Return to the island for lunch and a rest.
Times and order vary with the operator, weather and currents. Some shops reportedly offer an extra dive if no sharks are seen.
Travel from Cebu airport via the northern bus terminal to Maya port, take a bangka to the island and drop your bags at your lodging.
2–3 dawn thresher shark dives. Rest or enjoy the beach in the afternoon.
Dive at Gato Island or another site, or snorkel. Use it as a rest day depending on how you feel.
Leave the island and return to Cebu. Allow plenty of waiting time after your last dive before flying.
You need a waiting period after your last dive before boarding a flight. Follow the dive shop's advice when scheduling your flight.
Fly from Manila (MNL) to Mactan–Cebu International Airport (CEB). Check airline timetables.
Reviewers say the bus from Cebu's northern bus terminal to Maya port takes about 5–6 hours and costs about ₱220. Check schedules locally.
The shared bangka from Maya port to Malapascua takes about 30–45 minutes and is reported at about ₱100~240. An environmental fee and a terminal fee are charged separately.
Bus travel time depends heavily on traffic. Leave some slack in your schedule.
There are no cars on the island; people walk or ride motorbikes. Most lodging and dive shops are clustered around Bounty Beach.
The boat from the dive shop to Kimud Shoal leaves from the beach. It is dark at that hour, so bring a flashlight.

Threshers appear year-round, so a trip is possible almost any time, but the weather varies. One dive shop says March–May has the best weather, January–June is generally fine and August–December can be rough. Another review says December–July is the dry season with good weather and advises avoiding April–May, when tourists crowd the island.
Water temperature is given as about 28–30°C from March to December and about 26–27°C in January and February. If you dive in January or February, consider a thin wetsuit or hood.
If sea conditions are bad just before departure, the shop will delay or cancel the trip. In peak season bookings fill up days ahead, so confirm your date with the dive shop in advance.

Staying around Bounty Beach is the most convenient. Dive shops and restaurants are within walking distance, and it is easy to gather at dawn. Reviewers mention both resorts with a dive shop on the same property and resorts about a 10-minute walk from the beach. Wi-Fi is often weak and works only in common areas, so arrange any needed contact beforehand.

You eat at the beachfront restaurants. Most accept cash only, so exchange or withdraw money at Maya port or in Cebu beforehand. The island pharmacy may be closed or out of stock, so bring your own seasickness pills, sunscreen and insect repellent. One reviewer says the island pharmacy is cash-only with irregular hours. Reviewers also say a snorkeling trip around the island (about ₱500, varies by shop) can show baby blacktip sharks and sea turtles.
Getting an Advanced Open Water (AOW) certification lets you enjoy the widest range of dives. Open Water divers can sometimes join with an instructor for an extra fee.
Advertised prices may leave out the marine park fee, the Kimud fee and fuel, so ask for the total first.
The boat rocks at dawn, so bring seasickness pills and avoid heavy drinking the night before.
You need a waiting period after diving before you fly, so leave slack in your departure schedule.
Follow the rules that protect the sharks, including no flash or strobes.
If you have an underwater camera, practice settings that work without lights.
Bring plenty of cash. Few places on the island accept cards.
There are many shops, so compare their safety records, equipment maintenance and small-group operation.

Thresher dives are dawn dives down to about 20–30 m. Advanced certification or higher is recommended, so do not push yourself if your certification or condition is lacking. Fees and rules differ by shop, so confirm before booking.
Thresher sharks are wild animals. Do not chase or touch them or enter inside the rope line.
Leave enough time between your last dive and any flight. This is a basic rule to reduce the risk of decompression sickness.
Trips can be canceled because of weather. Build a spare day into your schedule.
Safety and equipment standards differ by shop. Check recent reviews and whether groups are kept small.
Even if a shop talks about a guarantee, sightings cannot be assured because these are wild animals. Some shops reportedly give an extra dive if you do not see any.
The island where the dive shops and beachfront lodging are clustered. You can also enjoy white sand beaches and snorkeling.
An island off northwest Cebu. If you want a beach break, it can be planned separately from Malapascua.
A dive town in southwest Cebu famous for sardine runs and turtles. A good place to split your itinerary with Malapascua.
The city that connects to the airport and the northern bus terminal. It is the starting point for the trip to Malapascua.
